property_summary: For every calldata layout used by the clone's immutable args, owner() returns the address encoded at offset 0x0 (the first encoded address); the mutant that reads offset 0x14 instead will return a different address for some calldata, so the property (owner()==address at offset 0x0) is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For any calldata layout (fuzzed bytes) passed as immutable args to the clone creation, the reference contract's owner() returns the address encoded at offset 0x0 of the immutable args; the mutant that reads offset 0x14 will sometimes return a different address, so owner()==address encoded at offset 0x0 is the invariant broken by the mutant.

For any two distinct addresses a and b passed as the first two encoded immutable args to the clone, the reference C.owner() always returns the first encoded address (a); the mutant that reads offset 0x14 returns the second address (b) and thus will differ for some fuzzed pair.

For any deployed C instance its owner() getter always returns the address encoded at immutable args offset 0x0; the mutant that reads offset 0x14 will sometimes return a different address (e.g. the collateral address) and thus violate this invariant.

For any bytes sequence used as the clone's immutable args, the correct contract's owner() returns the address encoded at offset 0x0 of those args, whereas the mutant that reads offset 0x14 can return a different address for some inputs (e.g. when the first and second encoded addresses differ).

For any deployed C instance, collateral() returns the immutable argument at calldata offset 0x14 (the second encoded address) — the mutant returns the first encoded address at 0x0, so for inputs where those two addresses differ the mutant will return a different address.

For any calldata layout used when creating the clone, calling collateral() on the correct contract returns the address encoded at the second immutable-arg slot (offset 0x14), whereas the mutant that reads offset 0x0 would return the first encoded address — therefore for some pairs of distinct addresses the mutant's collateral() return differs while the reference's does not.

For any two distinct addresses encoded into the clone creation immutable args (owner, collateral, ...), the correct C.collateral() always returns the second encoded address (the collateral arg) while the mutant that reads offset 0x0 would return the first encoded address — therefore for some fuzzed pair of addresses the returned ERC20 address differs; the property: collateral() returns an address equal to the second immutable-arg address.

For any calldata used to create the clone, the reference C.collateral() always returns the address encoded as the second immutable argument (offset 0x14), whereas the mutant that reads offset 0x0 will return the first immutable argument for some inputs — so the property is: collateral() returns the second encoded immutable address, and the mutant can break this when the first and second encoded addresses differ.

For any two distinct addresses encoded into the clone creation immutable args, the reference C.collateral() always returns the second encoded address (the collateral argument at offset 0x14); the mutant that reads offset 0x0 would instead return the first encoded address for some inputs, so the property is that collateral() equals the second encoded immutable address and the mutant can violate this when the first and second encoded addresses differ.
For any deployed C, collateral() always returns a non-zero ERC20 address (the creator-supplied collateral) — the mutant returns address(0) which violates this for some inputs.

For every call, the correct contract's collateral() returns a non-zero ERC20 address (non-zero address), whereas the mutant returns address(0) for some inputs, so collateral() != address(0) is a universal property violated by the mutant.

For every call, the correct C.collateral() returns an ERC20 whose address equals the immutable arg stored in the clone (non-zero for some fuzzed owner/collateral/debt/factory inputs), while the mutant returns address(0) breaking equality with the stored immutable arg for those inputs.

For any deployed C clone instance, calling collateral() should return the ERC20 address encoded in the contract's immutable args (i.e. a non-zero address when the encoded collateral arg is non-zero); the mutant always returns address(0) breaking this for inputs where the encoded immutable collateral arg is non-zero.

For any deployed C instance, calling collateral() must successfully return (i.e. not revert) an ERC20 address that is equal to the immutable-encoded collateral argument for that instance; the mutant always returns address(0) causing a difference for instances whose encoded collateral arg is non-zero (the call still succeeds but returns a different address).

For any deployed C, collateral() returns an ERC20 whose address equals the immutable collateral argument embedded at deployment; the mutant instead returns the factory address, so there exist inputs where collateral()'s returned address differs from the embedded collateral address.

For every deployed C instance, collateral() returns the ERC20 address that was embedded as the immutable collateral arg at deployment; the mutant returns the factory() address instead, so for some embedded collateral values the returned address will differ.

For any deployed C, collateral() always returns the ERC20 address embedded as the immutable collateral argument at deployment (the reference returns that embedded address for all inputs); the mutant returns factory()'s address instead, so for deployments where the embedded collateral arg != factory(), the mutant violates this rule.

For any deployed C instance, calling collateral() must return the ERC20 address that was embedded as the immutable collateral constructor argument (i.e., the stored immutable collateral arg), whereas the mutant returns factory()'s address instead and thus will differ for some embedded collateral arguments.

For any deployed C, collateral() must return the ERC20 address that was embedded as the immutable collateral constructor argument; the mutant returns the factory() address instead, so for some embedded collateral args the returned address differs.

For any deployed C, debt() always returns the immutable ERC20 address supplied at clone-time (non-zero for a properly initialized clone); the mutant returns address(0) breaking this by returning zero for some inputs.

For any input the reference C returns a non-zero ERC20 address from debt(), whereas the mutant returns address(0) for at least some inputs — so the general rule: debt() must return a nonzero address; the mutant violates this by returning address(0).
For any deployed reference C, calling debt() returns a nonzero ERC20 address (the immutable argument); the mutant instead can return the zero address, violating that rule.

For any deployed C clone the debt() getter returns an ERC20 whose address equals the immutable argument supplied at deployment (thus is equal to address(collateral()) only when that argument matches); the mutant that returns address(0) breaks this because for some fuzzed immutable argument values the returned address will be zero while the reference returns the provided (nonzero) address.

For any deployed reference C, calling debt() returns a non-zero ERC20 address (the immutable argument); the mutant returns the zero address for some inputs, so the property is that debt() != address(0) for all inputs, which the mutant violates for some inputs.

For any deployed C, debt() must return the immutable debt token address configured in the clone's immutable args (i.e., not equal to owner()); the mutant returns owner() (an address of owner cast to ERC20) breaking this rule for inputs where owner() != configured debt token.

For any deployed C instance constructed with its immutable args, debt() returns the configured ERC20 debt token address (not equal to owner()); the mutant makes debt() return owner(), so for inputs where owner() != configured debt token the mutant breaks this rule.

For any deployed C instance the public debt() getter always returns the immutable ERC20 debt token address encoded in the clone (not equal to owner()); the mutant returns owner() instead, so for inputs where owner() != configured debt token the mutant will return a different address and break this property.

For any deployed C instance created with its immutable args, the public debt() getter returns the ERC20 address encoded in the clone's immutable args (i.e., not equal to owner() for most inputs); the mutant returns owner() cast to ERC20 which makes debt() equal owner() for inputs where owner() != configured debt token, so the property is violated when those two addresses differ.

For any deployed C clone, the public debt() getter returns the ERC20 address encoded in the contract's immutable args; the mutant returns owner() (a different address) for some inputs where owner() != configured debt address, so the property is violated for those inputs.

For any deployed C, calling debt() returns the same address as the contract's immutable debt argument (distinct from collateral()) — the mutant makes debt() return collateral() instead, so there exist inputs where debt() == collateral(), violating the rule.

For any immutable constructor args, C.debt() returns the immutable-debt address encoded at offset 0x28 (i.e. is not equal to collateral()), whereas the mutant makes debt() return collateral(), so there exist fuzzed immutable arg bytes where debt() == collateral() and thus violates the rule.

For every deployed C the reference returns a debt() address that is not equal to collateral() (the immutable debt arg is independent); the mutant makes debt() equal collateral(), so there exist immutable constructor bytes where debt() == collateral(), violating the rule.

For any deployed C, the public getters collateral() and debt() must return the same address if and only if the immutable arg encoded at debt slot equals collateral's immutable arg; the reference implementation returns debt() from its distinct immutable slot (so for all inputs where the encoded immutable debt differs from the encoded immutable collateral the two getters differ), while the mutant always returns collateral() causing debt()==collateral() for some inputs where the reference would not, so there exist fuzzed immutable-arg bytes that make the mutant violate the inequality.

For any deployed C, the reference's debt() getter returns an ERC20 address unreachable by calling collateral() of the same instance when the encoded immutable debt address differs from the encoded immutable collateral address; the mutant instead returns collateral() always, so there exist constructor immutable-arg bytes (fuzzed) where debt() equals collateral(), violating the inequality.

For any 32-byte calldata word representing the stored immutable 'debt' address, the reference contract returns the address encoded in the low 20 bytes of that word (i.e. the calldata word right-shifted by 0x60), whereas the mutant returns the raw calldata word truncated to 20 bytes (casting uint256 directly), so when the high 12 bytes of the calldata word are nonzero the returned addresses differ; the reference always returns the value equal to address(uint160(shr(0x60, word))) but the mutant can return address(uint160(word)), violating that equality for some inputs.

For any 32-byte calldata word provided as the immutable `debt` argument, the reference contract's debt() returns the address encoded in the low 20 bytes of the word after shifting right by 0x60 (i.e. address(uint160(shr(0x60, word)))), while the mutant returns address(uint160(word)); thus the property is that debt() equals address(uint160(shr(0x60, word))) for every admissible calldata word — the mutant violates this for words whose high 12 bytes are nonzero.

For any 32-byte immutable-args calldata word representing the stored `debt` argument, the reference contract's debt() always returns address(uint160(shr(0x60, word))) (i.e. the low 20 bytes after shifting down), whereas the mutant returns address(uint160(word)) and thus can differ when the top 12 bytes of the calldata word are nonzero.

For any 32-byte immutable-args word provided as the stored `debt` argument, the reference C always returns debt() == address(uint160(shr(0x60, word))) (i.e. the address extracted by shifting the calldata word right by 0x60), while the mutant returns address(uint160(word)) and thus will differ for inputs where the top 12 bytes of the word are nonzero.

For any 32-byte immutable-args word used as the stored debt address, the reference C.debt() returns the address equal to address(uint160(shr(0x60, word))) (i.e. the calldata word right-shifted by 0x60 then lower 20 bytes); the mutant instead returns address(uint160(word)) and thus will differ when the high 12 bytes of the word are nonzero.

For any deployed reference C, factory() always returns the CoolerFactory address encoded in the immutable args (a non-zero address for clones created by the factory); the mutant instead returns address(0) which can differ for some inputs.

For any deployed C clone, calling factory() returns a non-zero CoolerFactory address (the reference encodes the factory in immutable args); the mutant returns address(0) breaking this rule for some inputs.

For any deployed C instance created via its constructor (not a clone) the factory() call should NOT return the zero address; the mutant returns address(0) for some inputs thus violating this property when called on such an instance.

For any deployed C instance constructed via its constructor, calling factory() returns a non-zero CoolerFactory address (the reference reads it from immutable args), whereas the mutant returns address(0) thus violating the non-zero factory invariant for some inputs.

For any deployed C instance constructed via its constructor, calling factory() should successfully return (not revert) the CoolerFactory address encoded in C's immutable args; the mutant instead returns address(0) (a different return value) for some inputs, so there exist inputs where the returned address differs — we assert the returned address is nonzero.

For every call, the correct contract's factory() returns the stored immutable CoolerFactory equal to the factory address embedded at clone creation (not equal to owner()); the mutant returns CoolerFactory(owner()), so there exist inputs where factory()'s returned address differs from owner() (i.e. factory() == CoolerFactory(address(c).owner()) is false for some inputs) — we assert that factory()'s address is not equal to owner() for all (fuzzed) owner values when owner() is not equal to the stored factory address, which the mutant will break by returning owner().

For any deployed C clone, factory() must return the CoolerFactory address stored in the immutable factory field (not equal to the owner() address for some owner values); the mutant that returns CoolerFactory(owner()) will make factory() equal owner() for those inputs, violating this rule.
